cim: AI will not replace the doctor. It will do something that might surprise you
cim_eredeti: AI will not replace the doctor. It will do something that might surprise you
szoveg_eredeti:
Before I became a doctor, I studied philosophy, economics, and political science. Ostensibly, a path far from medicine. But an article published recently in the New England Journal of Medicine reminded me just how much economics, in particular, can help us understand one of the most burning questions in medicine today: Is artificial intelligence about to replace doctors?

Dr. Dhruv Khullar, a physician and health policy researcher at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York, offers a surprising answer in the article. There is no doubt, he writes, that artificial intelligence will be able to perform more and more tasks currently carried out by medical professionals. And yet, it is very possible that the ultimate result will not be fewer medical professionals, but rather more medicine.

The first concept he recruits is called the "Jevons paradox." In 1865, the British economist William Stanley Jevons noticed that as steam engines became more efficient, coal consumption in England did not decrease, but skyrocketed: Efficiency made engines worthwhile in more and more places, and the increase in demand far exceeded the savings. The same thing happened in medicine. As cataract surgeries and joint replacements became safer and faster and required less doctor labor, they could be offered to more people. And radiology, the profession considered the first that AI would replace? There are more radiologists in the United States today than a decade ago, with a heavier workload.

The second concept is the "lump of labor fallacy": The tendency to imagine that there is a fixed amount of medical work in the world, and if AI performs a third of it, only two-thirds will remain for humans. However, technologies change prices, demand, and behavior, and create services and professions that did not exist before. Khullar argues that AI is expected to similarly create new modes of care and new specialties.

In my eyes, longevity medicine and preventive medicine are the best example of this.

The goal of longevity medicine is not only to extend life expectancy, but also health span: The number of years a person lives without chronic illness and without dependence on others. And our problem is not that there is not enough to do for this purpose. The problem is almost the opposite: There is too much. Truly personalized preventive medicine requires reviewing medical history, medications, laboratory tests, blood pressure, sleep, physical activity, screening tests, and vaccinations, and understanding what out of all this is truly important for the specific individual sitting in front of us. This is medicine that today is provided mainly in private clinics, to those who can pay for many doctor hours. There is not enough medical time in the public system to do this for millions of people.

And here AI can change the equation. Imagine a system that continuously reviews the medical record, identifies gaps in prevention, assesses risks, and suggests to the caregiver and patient the next action worth taking. It does not replace a visit that exists today. It adds an entire layer of proactive medicine, which today is almost impossible to provide at a population scale. This, for me, is the great promise of AI in a health fund: Democratization of longevity medicine. Not only for those who can pay, but for every insured person.

There is a deeper point here. Artificial intelligence is not just another device. It is infrastructure, like electricity or the internet: A layer deployed beneath every service that changes what can be built upon it. And I view longevity medicine this way as well: Not a boutique service, but infrastructure of the healthcare system, a layer of measurement, risk assessment, and prevention that needs to run in the background of every medical encounter, for every insured person, throughout life. Until today, such infrastructure required an impossible amount of human time. When connecting two infrastructures, one that knows how to process information at a population scale and one that knows what to do with it, the Jevons paradox stops being a theory and becomes a work plan.

But there is also a trap here. Medicine is not a collection of calculations. A caregiver needs to understand context, identify when the algorithm is wrong, talk with a person about their preferences, and sometimes decide not to do what the dry guideline suggests. Khullar uses the "O-ring theory" from economics here, named after the small rubber seal that failed and brought down the Space Shuttle Challenger: In a system of interdependent tasks, a failure in one small link can destroy the entire result. But there is also a second side to this: The better AI performs the analysis, the more the remaining human judgment will be worth, not less. Automation of medical tasks is not automation of the medical profession.

And this leads to a change that most healthcare systems have not yet prepared for. When the computer knows how to tell the patient what to do, the difficult question remains how to make them do it. Knowledge about nutrition, sleep, and physical activity is already available to everyone today, and most people do not change their behavior. This guidance will become hybrid: AI will do the daily layer of reminders and adaptation, health coaches will provide the commitment and trust that a person gives only to a human, and the doctor will become the person holding the entire picture: Knowing when the lifestyle plan conflicts with medications, identifying that fatigue is not a lack of motivation but an illness, bearing responsibility, and leading the team. Not by chance, in the list of skills that Khullar lists as un-automatable appear "motivating behavior change," "managing uncertainty," and "leading teams." And this means we will need to train doctors and caregivers for this, give them time for this, and reward them for this, and not only for visits and procedures.

Therefore, the question that healthcare system managers need to ask is not only how many doctor hours can be saved using AI. The truly interesting questions are how much more health can be generated with the same workforce, how many people we can reach before they become sick, and how many years of good health we can add to an entire population and not only to the few.

Perhaps in the end AI will indeed replace part of what doctors do today. Khullar does not claim otherwise either. But from the perspective of longevity, the more interesting possibility is different: The great revolution of artificial intelligence in medicine will not be that we will need fewer doctors, but that every doctor will be able to help many more people live more years in good health.

Dr. Nitzan Anav is a physician and head of longevity at Maccabi Healthcare Services.
